title: The Bed He Did Not Flee
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] Every account of the migration to Madinah fixates on the cave, the spider's web, the pursuers at its mouth, yet the more quietly extraordinary detail happened hours earlier, in a bed nobody remembers to mention.

Narrator: [reflective] Mecca's assassins, having agreed to strike simultaneously and thereby diffuse the guilt among many clans, surrounded the Prophet's house at night, expecting to find him asleep within.
Narrator: [serious] Ali ibn Abi Talib, still a young man, agreed instead to lie in that bed himself, draped in the Prophet's own cloak, fully aware of what discovery would almost certainly cost him.

Narrator: [analytical] What separates this from bravado is the deliberation involved, no impulsive dash toward danger, but a calculated night spent awaiting men assembled to kill whoever they found beneath that cloak.
Narrator: [thoughtful] He survived, the assassins having hesitated once uncertain, but the episode reveals something about Ali's character that outlasted that single night.
Narrator: [reflective] Decades later, as caliph during bitterly contested civil strife, he displayed a similarly deliberate refusal to seek advantage through methods conscience couldn't sanction.

Narrator: [analytical] Advisers urged him toward tactics his rivals employed without hesitation, and he consistently declined, insisting victory purchased through deception would corrode whatever legitimacy it claimed to secure.
Narrator: [with feeling] That restraint cost him militarily more than once, opponents exploiting scruples he refused to abandon even when abandoning them might have shortened a devastating conflict.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Some historians read that consistency as naivety, others as the same unwavering constancy first displayed in a stranger's bed decades earlier.

Narrator: [reflective] I find myself persuaded by the latter, if only because the two episodes rhyme so precisely, accepting personal cost rather than compromise a principle he refused to treat as negotiable.

Narrator: [with feeling] He was assassinated eventually, struck while praying, echoing uncomfortably how his life had nearly ended decades before, danger arriving while he remained most exposed and most devoted.

Narrator: [warmly] What I find instructive isn't the martial reputation history remembers, but that earlier decision, a young man choosing someone else's danger over his own safety, then spending the rest of his life refusing to unlearn it.

quiz.question: What did Ali agree to do on the night of the migration to Madinah?
options: Flee the city immediately
Lie in the Prophet's bed, draped in his cloak, fully aware of the danger
Warn the assassins of the plan
Hide in the cave instead
quiz.explanation: Ali agreed to lie in the Prophet's bed, draped in his cloak, fully aware of what discovery could cost him.

quiz.question: Why did the assassins plan to strike simultaneously?
options: To make the attack faster
To diffuse the guilt of a single killer among many clans
Because they were unsure of the house's location
To avoid detection by guards
quiz.explanation: They agreed to strike simultaneously specifically to diffuse the guilt of a single killer among many clans.

quiz.question: What distinguishes Ali's action from simple bravado, according to the narrator?
options: It was entirely spontaneous
It involved deliberation, a calculated night awaiting men assembled to kill whoever lay beneath the cloak
It required no risk at all
It was ordered by someone else
quiz.explanation: The narrator emphasizes the deliberation involved, not an impulsive dash but a calculated acceptance of danger.

quiz.question: How did Ali later behave as caliph regarding tactics his rivals used?
options: He adopted the same tactics readily
He consistently declined tactics his conscience couldn't sanction, even at military cost
He avoided conflict entirely
He delegated all decisions to advisers
quiz.explanation: He consistently declined deceptive tactics his rivals used, insisting victory through deception would corrode legitimacy, even when it cost him militarily.

quiz.question: How does the narrator connect Ali's death to the earlier bed episode?
options: They are entirely unrelated
Both involve danger arriving while he remained most exposed and most devoted
He died of natural causes instead
He was killed by the same people
quiz.explanation: The narrator notes his assassination while praying echoes the earlier episode, danger arriving while he was most exposed and devoted.
